legal.privacy_p1: Congruent Solutions, Inc. ("we", "us", or "our") respects your privacy. This Privacy Policy describes how we collect, use, disclose, and safeguard your information when you use this participant portal and related retirement plan services.
legal.privacy_p2: We collect information you provide directly (such as account registration details), information related to your employer-sponsored plan as permitted by law, and technical data such as device and usage information to operate and secure the service. We use this information to administer your plan, comply with legal obligations, communicate with you, and improve our services.
legal.privacy_p3: We do not sell your personal information. We may share information with service providers who assist in plan administration, as required by law, or with your consent. You may have rights regarding access, correction, or deletion of certain information depending on your jurisdiction. For questions about this policy, contact your plan administrator or our support team.

legal.terms_p2: The portal is provided to help you view and manage your retirement plan information. Features may change over time. You are responsible for safeguarding your login credentials and for the accuracy of information you submit.
legal.terms_p3: To the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, the service is provided "as is" without warranties of any kind. Nothing in these terms alters any rights or obligations set forth in your plan documents, summary plan description, or agreements between you, your employer, and the plan.
legal.help_p1: Find answers about enrollment, contributions, investments, loans, withdrawals, and using this portal. If you cannot find what you need, our support team is here to help.
legal.help_p2: For account-specific questions (including personal balance, transactions, or employer plan rules), contact your plan administrator or HR department. For technical issues signing in or using this website, email our support team using the address below.

enrich.title: Enrich
enrich.subtitle: Financial wellness library
enrich.intro: Guides and short lessons to help you make confident decisions about your plan and retirement.
enrich.path_desc: A 4-part guide covering enrollment, deferral sources, employer match and your first investment election.
enrich.educational: General education, not personal financial, tax or legal advice. Check your plan documents for the rules that apply to you.
enrich.empty: No articles in this topic yet.

enrolling.title: How enrolling works
enrolling.summary: What you decide when you enroll, and what you can change later.
body: When you enroll, you choose how much of each paycheck to save and how those savings are invested. You also decide whether each dollar goes in before taxes (pre-tax) or after taxes (Roth).
Nothing you pick is permanent. You can change your deferral rate and your investments whenever you like, and many plans let you raise your rate automatically each year.
The most helpful step is simply to start. Even a small percentage grows over time, and you can increase it as your budget allows.

sources.title: Deferral sources
sources.summary: Pre-tax, Roth and the other places money in your account can come from.
body: Your account can hold money from different sources. The ones you control are pre-tax deferrals, which lower your taxable pay today, and Roth deferrals, which you pay tax on now but can withdraw tax-free in retirement if the rules are met.
Other sources, like employer match or profit sharing, are added by your employer. Each source can have its own rules for when you can use the money.
You can split your deferral between pre-tax and Roth. Your balance by source is shown on your account summary.

match.title: Employer match
match.summary: How matching works and why it's worth capturing in full.
body: Many employers add money to your account when you save, usually matching a share of what you contribute up to a limit. That match is extra compensation you only receive if you contribute enough.
A common goal is to contribute at least as much as it takes to get the full match. Your plan documents show the formula.
Matching money may be subject to a vesting schedule, which sets when it becomes fully yours. Your vested balance shows the portion you keep if you leave.

first_election.title: Your first investment election
first_election.summary: Choosing where your savings go, in plain terms.
body: An investment election is how you split your savings across the funds your plan offers. The percentages must add up to 100%.

If you'd rather not pick individual funds, many people choose a target-date fund, which adjusts its mix as your retirement date approaches. You can also answer a short questionnaire to match a mix to your comfort with risk.
Review your election now and then. Your goals and your timeline change, and a quick check keeps your mix on track.

understanding_401k.title: Understanding your 401(k)
understanding_401k.summary: How deferrals, employer match and vesting work together.
body: A 401(k) lets you save part of your pay for retirement through your employer. Your deferrals come out of your paycheck and go into investments you choose.
Employer match adds to your savings, and vesting decides how much of that match you own over time. Your own deferrals are always fully yours.
There is a yearly limit on how much you can defer, set by the IRS. People 50 and older can usually add a catch-up amount. Your account shows how much of the limit is left this year.

pretax_vs_roth.title: Pre-tax vs Roth deferrals
pretax_vs_roth.summary: Compare the two and when each can make sense.
body: Pre-tax deferrals reduce your taxable income now, and you pay income tax when you withdraw. Roth deferrals are taxed now, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
One way to think about it is the tax rate you expect to pay later compared with today. If you expect a higher rate in retirement, Roth may appeal. If you expect a lower one, pre-tax may.
You don't have to choose just one. Splitting between the two gives you flexibility. A tax professional can help with your own situation.

investing_basics.title: Investment basics
investing_basics.summary: Asset classes, target-date funds and why diversification matters.
body: Asset classes such as stocks and bonds behave differently. Stocks have tended to grow more over long periods but move up and down more. Bonds are usually steadier with lower growth.
Diversification means spreading your savings across different funds so no single one decides your outcome. Target-date funds do this for you and shift toward more stable investments over time.
Fees matter too. A fund's expense ratio is what it costs each year, and lower costs leave more of your return working for you.

planning.title: Planning for retirement
planning.summary: Estimate what you'll need and set realistic goals.
body: Start with what you expect to spend each month in retirement, then compare it with your expected income from savings, Social Security and anything else you'll have.
If there's a gap, you have levers: save more, retire a little later, or adjust your spending goal. Raising your savings rate by a point or two now can make a real difference over time.
Include savings outside your 401(k), like IRAs or brokerage accounts. The retirement readiness tool lets you try different numbers and see the effect.

projected_balance.title: Projected retirement balance
projected_balance.body: An estimate of what your account could be worth when you retire if you keep saving like this. It's a guide, not a promise.
projected_balance.more: It adds up what you and your employer put in each year and assumes your investments grow at an average rate for the risk profile you picked. Real returns go up and down, so treat it as a rough picture. Saving a little more, or starting earlier, makes the biggest difference.

contribution_rate.title: Contribution rate
contribution_rate.body: The share of each paycheck you save into your 401(k). It's also called your deferral rate.
contribution_rate.more: If you earn $5,000 a paycheck and choose 6%, $300 goes into your account before you're paid. You can change it later. The IRS limits how much you can contribute each year.

employer_match.title: Employer match
employer_match.body: Money your employer adds when you save. Your plan matches what you put in, up to {{cap}}% of your pay. That limit is the match cap.
employer_match.more: If you earn $60,000 and save {{cap}}% ($3,600 a year), your employer adds $3,600 too. Saving less than {{cap}}% leaves some of that money unused, so many people save at least up to the match cap.

tax_treatment.title: Pre-tax and Roth
tax_treatment.body: Pre-tax savings lower your taxes now, and you pay tax when you take the money out. Roth savings are taxed now, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
tax_treatment.more: Pre-tax often suits people who expect a lower tax rate in retirement. Roth often suits people early in their career, or who expect higher taxes later. A mix of both spreads the bet. Roth withdrawals are tax-free once you're 59½ and your first Roth contribution was at least five years earlier.

plan_deferral_rate.title: Plan deferral rate
plan_deferral_rate.body: The default contribution rate your employer set for the plan. Choosing it uses that rate instead of one you pick.
plan_deferral_rate.more: It's a starting point, not a recommendation for everyone. If it's below the match cap, you won't get the full employer match.

auto_increase.title: Auto-increase
auto_increase.body: Raises your contribution rate by a small amount each year until it reaches the limit you set.
auto_increase.more: For example, start at 6% and go up 1% a year until you reach 10%. Small steps are easier to absorb than one big jump, especially if they line up with a pay raise. You can turn it off at any time.

increment_cycle.title: When increases happen
increment_cycle.body: The date each year your auto-increase takes effect: January 1, the date you enrolled, or the start of the plan year (April 1).
increment_cycle.more: Many people pick the date closest to their yearly pay raise, so the increase is barely noticed. This only changes when the increase happens, not how much it is.

sources.title: Sources
sources.body: Each type of money in your account, such as pre-tax and Roth, is tracked separately as a source.
sources.more: With "Apply to all sources" ticked, pre-tax and Roth money go into the same funds. Untick it to choose different funds for each. Auto-increase can also use a different amount for each source.

invest_mode.title: Ways to invest
invest_mode.body: "Match my comfort with risk" picks a fund mix for the risk profile you choose. "Let the plan choose" uses your employer's default mix. "Choose my own funds" lets you pick everything.
invest_mode.more: If you're not sure, matching your comfort with risk is a good place to start. You can change your investments at any time after you enroll.

risk_profile.title: Risk profile
risk_profile.body: How much up and down in your account value you're comfortable with. Higher-risk mixes hold more stocks: they can grow more over time but fall more in bad years.
risk_profile.more: Conservative holds more bonds and changes less. Aggressive holds mostly stocks. People with many years until retirement often choose more growth, because they have time to recover from downturns. The short questionnaire can suggest a profile.

allocation.title: Allocation
allocation.body: How your savings are split between funds, as percentages that must add up to 100%.
allocation.more: For example, 60% in a stock fund and 40% in a bond fund means $60 of every $100 you save goes to stocks. Spreading money across several funds limits the effect of any one fund doing badly.

expense_ratio.title: Expense ratio
expense_ratio.body: The yearly fee a fund charges, as a percentage of what you have invested in it.
expense_ratio.more: 0.04% means $4 a year for every $10,000 invested. It's taken out of the fund's returns, so you never get a bill. Lower fees leave more of your money growing, which adds up over decades.

auto_rebalance.title: Auto rebalance
auto_rebalance.body: Every quarter, moves money between your funds to bring them back to the percentages you chose.
auto_rebalance.more: Funds grow at different speeds, so a 60/40 mix can drift to 70/30 over time. Rebalancing keeps your risk at the level you chose.

sdb.title: Self-Directed Brokerage
sdb.body: An optional brokerage account in your plan for investing in a wider range of funds and stocks than the plan's list.
sdb.more: It's meant for experienced investors. It can carry extra fees, and you choose and keep track of every investment yourself. Most people don't need it.
